evidence_collisions.cost_if_wrong: C2 lengthens the bodice or raises the waistline (AF-11); C3 adds abdominal volume (AF-13). A length change made for a girth shortage leaves the shortage.

evidence_collisions.shared_observation: Diagonal drag lines from the sleeve cap toward the bicep, worse when the arm is raised.
evidence_collisions.why_it_fails: C1's evidence is 'the lines are concentrated at the bicep line; they increase markedly when the arm is raised' - the second half is the observation restated. More fundamentally, cap height (C2) and bicep width (C1) are not independent: they trade off along the same armhole circumference, so a pattern with an over-high cap IS a pattern with a narrow bicep at that armhole. The file asserts a separation the geometry does not support.
evidence_collisions.cost_if_wrong: C1 widens the sleeve; C2 lowers and widens the cap; C3 enlarges the armhole and only then re-measures. C3's own order note ('AF-08 must be settled before AF-09') implies these cannot be tested in the listed order.

evidence_collisions.shared_observation: Vertical slack folds in the upper sleeve; the sleeve hangs like a bag; the arm moves freely.
evidence_collisions.why_it_fails: C1's evidence is 'the folds are vertical; arm movement is completely free'. A deliberately full sleeve (C2) gives vertical folds and free movement. C1 does not exclude the design.
evidence_collisions.cost_if_wrong: The reader narrows a sleeve that is correct as designed.

evidence_collisions.shared_observation: Both sleeves twisting in the same direction, the underarm seam spiralling.
evidence_collisions.why_it_fails: C1's evidence is 'the twist is in the SAME direction on both sleeves'. A forward arm carriage - the sleeve-pitch mismatch that C2 describes - is bilateral and produces exactly that. C1's second marker (cap notches not matching the shoulder seam) does work, but it is stated as an addition rather than as the test.
evidence_collisions.cost_if_wrong: Also a routing fault: C1's likelihood_note calls it an ASSEMBLY error ('KALIP DEGIL, MONTAJ hatasi') but assigns adjustment_family_ref AF-09, which the schema reserves for pattern adjustments - the schema's own comment says null means 'this cause is NOT a pattern adjustment (e.g. a construction error)'. SYM-034.C3 breaks the same rule. Separately, the record omits FORWARD SHOULDER (AF-05) as a candidate, although the practitioner literature links forward shoulder posture directly to sleeve rotation.

evidence_collisions.shared_observation: Horizontal drag lines below the seat with the crotch pulling up.
evidence_collisions.why_it_fails: Crotch depth is a component of crotch length; the two measurements (M-026, M-027) are not independent. C1's own physical test - 'increase the crotch depth at the lengthen line' - also increases the back crotch length, so performing C1's test cannot distinguish C1 from C2: it relieves both. Under step 6 the reader would conclude 'the symptom disappeared, hypothesis confirmed' for whichever cause they happened to test first.
evidence_collisions.cost_if_wrong: Adding depth when the shortage is in the back crotch curve lowers the crotch on a body that did not need it, and the record's own order note (AF-15 before AF-16) then locks the error in.

evidence_collisions.shared_observation: Fabric pooling in a 'U' at the front crotch, back clean.
evidence_collisions.why_it_fails: C3's evidence is 'the NUMBERS ARE CORRECT but the curve is too deep'. A deeper front crotch curve necessarily lengthens the front crotch seam, which is the number C1 measures. 'Numbers correct, curve too deep' is therefore not a state the two measurements can jointly report, and C1's evidence ('pooling in front, back clean') is equally true of C3.
evidence_collisions.cost_if_wrong: C1 shortens the front crotch seam, C3 flattens the curve - two different alterations of the same seam separated by a criterion the measurement cannot deliver.

evidence_collisions.shared_observation: Both trouser legs twisting, evident standing.
evidence_collisions.why_it_fails: C1's evidence is 'the twist is symmetric on both legs and evident standing'. An unbalanced front/back crotch curve (C2) is a pattern fault and therefore bilateral and evident standing. C2's marker ('the twist starts at crotch level') is exclusive; C1 has none.
evidence_collisions.cost_if_wrong: Shifting the knee-level inseam/outseam balance (C1) on a trouser whose real fault is at the crotch moves the twist rather than removing it.

evidence_collisions.shared_observation: The crotch hanging low and away from the body, making it hard to stride.
evidence_collisions.why_it_fails: C1's evidence is 'the gap between crotch and body is present standing; comfortable sitting'. A deliberately dropped crotch (C2) gives the same. A waistband sitting below the natural waist (C3) drops the crotch with it and gives the same. C1 is satisfied by all three.
evidence_collisions.cost_if_wrong: Reducing crotch depth (C1) when the waistband is simply sitting low (C3) shortens a rise that was correct, and the trouser then binds when the waistband is worn at the intended level.

evidence_collisions.shared_observation: The garment rotating consistently in one direction on the body.
evidence_collisions.why_it_fails: C1's evidence is 'the rotation is consistent in one direction and the same at every wearing'. Body asymmetry (C2) also rotates consistently in one direction at every wearing. C2 adds 'together with one-sided signs' but C1 does not require their absence.
evidence_collisions.cost_if_wrong: Low - both route to AF-13 - but the symmetric fix and the asymmetric fix are different operations.

evidence_collisions.shared_observation: The centre-front or centre-back line not hanging perpendicular to the floor.
evidence_collisions.why_it_fails: C1's evidence is 'the deviation is symmetric and persists in the reader's natural stance'. A volume pulling the fabric (C2) is symmetric and persists in the natural stance. C2's marker ('the deviation starts at the level of that volume') is exclusive; C1 has none.
evidence_collisions.cost_if_wrong: High leverage, because SYM-042 is the record the whole balance step rests on: a shoulder balance correction (C1) applied when the true cause is bust or seat volume moves the balance lines without removing the cause, and every reading taken afterwards is then taken on a garment that has been altered for the wrong reason.

evidence_collisions.shared_observation: One dimension is the wrong length and there is no other sign at all.
evidence_collisions.why_it_fails: C1's evidence is 'the garment sits correctly everywhere, balance lines correct, no drag or fold - ONLY the length differs'. A deliberate design length (C2) and a differently folded hem allowance (C3) both produce exactly that. C3 adds a quantitative marker (the difference equals the hem allowance) and C2 a documentary one; C1 excludes neither.
evidence_collisions.cost_if_wrong: Low. Note that SYM-043 is otherwise the best-constructed record in the file: it is the ONLY one whose origin_rule states an explicit validity gate ('if any other sign is present this record is INVALID - diagnose the other sign first'). That gate is the pattern the other 42 records need.

top_risks.why: Two of the book's four core rules are cited to a document that does not contain them. I obtained EM4582 at the exact URL in the project's own source record and read all eight pages: it carries CC-23 almost verbatim and CC-26 verbatim, and it contains NO fold-axis rule (CC-22), NO drag-line content of any kind (CC-24) and no statement that the hem is read last or is derivative (CC-29). S-0004 is a source_ref on all 43 signs. The fix is available and cheap: WSU published a real fitting document, E.M. 2246 'Garment Fitting' (1962), which is reachable, carries a full sign-to-cause list, and settles several of the questions this book is asking.

The most-used rule in the book is (a) not in the source it cites - I read EM4582 in full and it contains no fold-axis rule - and (b) stated in a form that has no cell for a taut horizontal wrinkle. The book's own data proves the second point: three of the five records classed horizontal_fold describe shortage, not surplus, and SYM-027's own origin_rule states the counterexample outright. A reader who applies the Chapter-7 table to SYM-027 or SYM-035 will shorten a garment that is too narrow - the exact failure the claim's own risk_note names. The fix is small and additive: read slack-or-taut before horizontal-or-vertical, note that the axis inverts between them, and re-point the citation.

Step 4 of the seven-step cycle (LOCALIZE) has no mechanism other than this claim. Its cited source contains nothing about drag lines at all - I read EM4582 in full. The authorities that do discuss them offer three incompatible geometries (points toward / radiates from / runs between two named points), the mechanics say a drag line is a segment with two ends rather than an arrow, the project's own terminology entry T-13 states the opposite direction from CC-24, and two of the book's own records (SYM-004, SYM-037) are counterexamples. The visual token TK-05 draws it as an arrowhead, which the geometry does not license.

Largest cost-to-cause mismatch found. A gap at bust level with the closure clean above and below is C1's evidence verbatim AND the necessary consequence of C3 (no button at apex level). The reader who stops at C1 performs a full bust adjustment when the correct fix is moving one button. Fixable by making the button-position check a gate rather than a third alternative.

C1 and C2 prescribe opposite adjustments of the same magnitude at the same point (raise the shoulder tip 5-10 mm / lower it 5-10 mm), separated by a criterion the reader cannot apply: the 'direction' of a diagonal line. This is the one collision where following the wrong branch actively worsens the fit. It is also the one with a ready-made fix: WSU E.M. 2246 separates the two faults by ENDPOINTS and TENSION - square shoulders give taut diagonals from the SHOULDER TIP to centre front or back, sloping shoulders give slanting FOLDS from the BASE OF THE NECK to the underarm - and the record's current observation is the sloping sign, with a square-shoulder cause filed under it.

The method's most-quoted safety rule - pin, fold, add a strip, do NOT cut - is violated by 17 of the 129 candidate causes, three of which cut a neckline that SYM-001's own do_not_change_yet declares unrestorable. Either the rule is too strong for a toile or 13 percent of the test set must be rewritten; the book cannot ship holding both.

Three independent authorities - the book's own cited E-372, Palmer/Pletsch and Cynthia Guffey - agree with each other that fitting begins at the shoulder and neck, and disagree with 'begins with grain and balance'. The supporting citation is also miscounted (the checklist has 14 items, not 13) and is a checklist rather than a sequence. The claim can be kept if it is separated into order-of-READING (the book's own, unsourced) and order-of-CORRECTING (top-down, sourced).

CC-29 asserted as data. All three candidate causes are faults above the hem; bias drop in flared and bias-cut garments and off-grain cutting - both attested in extension publications, and one of them the reason the 24-hour hang exists - appear only as confounders. A reader with a correctly drafted circle skirt is routed to a full bust adjustment.

The observation string combines two opposite armhole faults ('binds when the arm is lowered' = armhole too high; 'the garment is pulled up from the shoulder' = armhole too low). C1's remedy lowers the underarm, which moves the garment toward the second fault. Split the record.

Not one of the 20 confounder-class or design-intent causes is listed first in its sign; 13 are last and 7 second. Step 6 tells the reader to test one hypothesis and to test the cheapest first, and readers work down lists - so the ordering systematically defers the free reversible check behind a pattern alteration. SYM-029 states the correct order in its own origin_rule and then violates it in the same object. This is the cheapest high-value correction in the dataset and needs no new research.

could_not_verify: Galada, A. & Baytar, F. (2025), Fashion and Textiles 12(1), DOI 10.1186/s40691-025-00417-y — FULL TEXT. I verified the article's existence, authors, journal, DOI, CC-BY licence and reference list (which includes Veblen 2012 and Liechty/Rasband/Pottberg-Steineckert 2016) through DOI content negotiation, but link.springer.com redirects to an identity provider and fashionandtextiles.springeropen.com redirects back to it, so I could not read the body. Two sentences attributed to this paper in my CC-22 and CC-24 findings — 'Vertical folds imply excess circumference measurement and horizontal folds imply excess vertical measurement' and 'Draglines are horizontal or diagonal pulls that radiate from a location that is too tight or does not have adequate 3D shaping' — reached me second-hand from a sub-researcher who states they fetched it. They are the best available modern sourcing for CC-22 and should be confirmed against the paper before printing. My own conclusions do not depend on them.

SDSU Extension Circular, 'Facts about Fitting' (1968), openprairie.sdstate.edu — reported to contain the most precise drag-line rule found anywhere ('If there is a group of wrinkles they will generally point in the direction of the seam to be let out. A line drawn at right angles from the center of a diagonal wrinkle will point to the seam to be taken in'). I did NOT reach it; the quote is second-hand. If it holds it is the closest thing to a source for CC-24 and should be obtained.

Texas AgriLife single-topic alteration leaflets E-375 (Bodice Back Width), E-376, E-377, E-383 (Upper Arm Sleeve Width) and E-384 — the same series as the book's own S-0003, reported to contain further horizontal-wrinkle-from-tightness counterexamples and one direct source-vs-source conflict on the hollow chest (E-376 horizontal folds vs WSU EC 306 lengthwise wrinkles). oaktrust.library.tamu.edu returns HTTP 403 to WebFetch and to curl with a browser user-agent; I did not reach any of them and cite none of them.

Threads Magazine, 'Fitting Revelations: Read Your Clothes to Identify Key Fit Issues' - the four-cell wrinkle rule (tight/loose x horizontal/vertical) reached me only through a search-engine extract. threadsmagazine.com returns HTTP 403 to WebFetch and to curl with a browser user-agent; I could not read the article body. The four-cell structure is independently corroborated by Yang & Baytar (2024), so the finding does not rest on it, but the specific wording must not be quoted as verified.

Texas A&M AgriLife 'Shoulder Slope' publication (oaktrust.library.tamu.edu/bitstream/handle/1969.1/87753/pdf_693.pdf) - HTTP 403 to WebFetch and to curl with a browser UA. This is the document that would settle whether square shoulders present as diagonal drag lines (as SYM-004 asserts) or as horizontal wrinkling across the upper back (as practitioner summaries report). I record the conflict; I could not resolve it.

Wild Ginger, 'Solving Fit Issues' (Shanley & Campbell), wildginger.com/pdffiles/pmfittingguide.pdf - connection refused (ECONNREFUSED). Repeatedly surfaced in searches as a systematic wrinkle-diagnosis reference; not read.

Not obtained; only its bibliographic description and publisher copy were seen. The six-cell taxonomy is therefore verified at one remove, through a peer-reviewed paper that cites it, not from the text itself.
Utah Education Network CTE handout S5_PatternAlterationsTips.pdf - HTTP 404.

(1969), 'Analysis of the Fit of Women's Custom-Made Pants', M.S. thesis, Oregon State University - reported to me by a sub-researcher as showing that total-crotch-length measurement predicts the needed alteration significantly better than crotch-depth measurement (tailor's square accurate for 22.2 percent of garments). I could NOT retrieve this document and do not cite its numbers. Worth the author obtaining from ScholarsArchive@OSU.

Texas A&M AgriLife E-390 'Special Alterations for Pants' and B-1295, and UNL Extension EC69-455 - the trouser-diagnosis publications that would most directly test SYM-027, SYM-035 and SYM-036. All returned 403/503.
Palmer/Pletsch, 'Pants for Real People' - the primary practitioner authority for SYM-035 and SYM-036. Only the publisher's fitting excerpt from a different title was obtainable.

Whether 'sway back' as used in fitting is the same condition as 'sway back posture' in kinesiology (which denotes posterior pelvic tilt with a FLATTENED lumbar spine, not the lumbar hollow the sewing sense implies). The book uses the sewing sense throughout; the possible collision with the clinical term is unresolved and matters because readers will search the clinical term. Not settled from documents.

THE CENTRAL UNVERIFIABLE ITEM, stated plainly: the 129 distinguishing_evidence fields are the book's actual product, and no documentary source distinguishes two causes of the SAME sign from each other. The project says this itself (SOURCE_MAP.md section 6; DIAGNOSTIC_SYSTEM.md section 6.4) and I confirm it independently - I found no publication that sets out competing causes for one observed sign with a discriminating test for each. Every collision I report is therefore an INTERNAL-LOGIC finding: it shows that the stated evidence cannot do the job the schema requires of it. Whether a corrected evidence field would discriminate on a real body is REQUIRES_PHYSICAL_TEST for all 129 and cannot be settled from documents.
